# Playing together on mindblown

A page where more than one person is in the same place at once -- a table, a
match, a shared board, everybody moving at once or one at a time. This is the
part of the SDK (`references/sdk.md` in the `mindblown` skill) for that, and only that. Everything here is
`window.mindblown` (`mb` below), the same object the SDK describes.

**Read this whole file before writing the first line of a page that seats two
people.** Two things are different from every other page: the rules of your
page run in a file that runs on the server, and your page draws what the
server says rather than what it worked out itself. The rules in here are the
ones the server enforces, and a refusal will name this file.

## The shape

Your page ships two things:

- **`rules.js`** at the root of your bundle, served at `https://<your-host>/rules.js`.
  The room fetches it when a room opens and runs it. It has no DOM, no
  network, no clock of its own. It is the rules, and nothing else.
- **The page**, which draws the lobby and the match, and sends the seat's
  input. It decides nothing about the match, and nothing about how people get
  to it: which room, the join and the start are ours.

The room runs `step` twenty times a second and sends each seat what `view`
says that seat may see. Everybody draws the same match because everybody is
drawing the room's answer.

**Send one input per tick, which is twenty a second.** The room keeps the LAST
input per seat and clears them as the tick runs, so a second message in the
same tick replaces the first and anything beyond one per tick is thrown away by
construction. Thirty a second is what the limiter tolerates, not a rate worth
aiming at: it cannot make the match more responsive, and on a weak connection
it is the traffic that makes it worse. Send at the tick rate or below, and
predict locally between ticks.

## The lobby and the match

**We run the room. Your page draws it.** Which room, the join, who is present
and when the match starts are the platform's. How all of it looks is yours.

```js
mb.live.lobby((state) => drawLobby(state));   // every change before the start
mb.live.match((channel) => play(channel));    // once, when every seat is here
playButton.onclick = () => mb.live.play({ public: true, seats: 2 });
```

Register both on load, every load. Then:

- **A link joins by itself.** When the address carries `?room=`, we join that
  room the moment you register `match`. Do not read the address and do not
  show a start screen first: the person followed a link to somebody, and the
  lobby of that room is what they should see.
- **A page can open already in its room.** Some places open your page for a
  group of people who are already together, and give all of them one room.
  The address then carries `?room=` from the first load, as a link does. Show
  that room's lobby at once. Do not show a menu for somebody alone: no solo
  start, no public match, no private room to open. Every join from that page
  sits in that room, whatever it asks for.
- **`play(opts)` is your own button.** `{ public: true, seats: N }` puts them
  with people; `{ seats: N }` opens a room of their own to share. We write the
  room into the address, so a reload is the same seat.
- **A full room starts.** We call `match` once, when every seat is connected,
  and not before. Never put a Ready button, an invite control or a share
  prompt in front of it -- nobody is missing.

`state` is data, and every pixel of it is yours to draw:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `room` | the room's name |
| `seats` | how many it holds |
| `mine` | this person's seat, from 1 |
| `present` | `[{ seat, username, mine }]` -- who is connected now |
| `link` | the link to send, already made with `mb.shareUrl` |
| `refused` | absent, or `{ reason, needsAccount }` -- show it; see [Refusals](#refusals) |

The channel `match` hands you is described under [`mb.live`](#mblive):
`channel.room` is the room with everybody named, `channel.seat` is yours.

```js
leaveButton.onclick = () => mb.live.leave();   // closes the socket, frees the seat
```

**`leave` is a control, never a lifecycle event.** Closing a tab is going
offline, not leaving; the match is still theirs. Do not call it on `pagehide`,
`unload` or a reload.

`mb.room.join` and `mb.live.join` are the calls under these, and they still
answer. Do not use them in a new page: every piece of arrival and start logic a
page wrote around them is what this section replaced.

## The room is the authority

**Every fact about a room comes back from the room, and from nowhere else.**

| What you want to know | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- |
| how many seats this table has | `room.seats` |
| which seat is mine | `room.mine` |
| whose turn it is | `room.turn` |
| who else is here | `room.seated` |
| what the table looks like | `room.state` |
| what I am holding | `room.private` |

Never from your own address, never from a message another page sent, never
from what somebody typed, never from what your page asked for a moment ago.
Those are one thing: a value somebody else can set.

```js
mb.live.match((channel) => layOutTable(channel.room.seats));   // the room's answer
```

`seats` is read when a room is opened and never again. A later arrival is
seated at the size the room already has, whatever it asks for.

**Or ask for a room with people in it, and we find one.**

```js
mb.live.play({ public: true, seats: 4 });
```

`public` means *put me somewhere with people*: we take the fullest open room of
your page that still has a seat, and open one when there is nowhere to sit. When
your address carries `?room=` and that room is public with a free seat, it is
the one we take -- the person followed a link to somebody, and that is who they
sit with. `seats` is still the size, and is used only if this ask is the one
that opens a room. The answer is the same room you always get, so everything after it is
unchanged: put `room.name` in a link and you can still invite anybody you like
into it.

**A public room is public because you said so when you opened it.** Nobody
picks one from a list; a person asks and the server seats them. Asking twice
returns the room you are in, so a reload is not a second seat.

**Tell an arrival that somebody is waiting.** Before anybody presses your
button, you can ask who is in a public room of your page right now with a seat
free:

```js
const waiting = await mb.live.waiting();
// [{ room: "quiet_lake_41", seats: 2, present: [{ username: "ada", waited_s: 40 }] }]
if (waiting.length) say(`${waiting[0].present[0].username} is waiting -- play now`);
playButton.onclick = () => mb.live.play({ public: true, seats: 2 });
```

It is for SHOWING, not for choosing. Join with the same `play({ public: true })`:
we seat the person in the first room of that list, which is the fullest. Never
pass one of these names as `room` to steer somebody into it, and never offer
the list as a menu -- that is matchmaking of your own, and it spreads people
across rooms. A named room is never in the list, the person asking is never in
it, and an empty list means nobody is waiting; draw nothing then. People wait
seconds, not minutes, so ask when the page opens and again when your start
screen comes back, not on a timer.

**Asking for a room while you are in one gives you that room.** Pressing your
own Play button twice is one room and not two. A page that wants a SECOND room
calls `mb.live.leave()` first, then `play` again.

**A seat in a public room is held while you are there, and is free when you are
not.** Close the tab and your seat goes back to the pool within about a minute;
come back and you are seated with whoever is playing now, which is what asking
for a public room meant. This is the one place a seat behaves differently from
a named room, where the seat stays yours.

**So do not write your own matchmaking, and delete it if you have.** You can
see only the room you were handed, never the pool, so the only move available
to you is to refuse one and open another -- which spreads the people you were
trying to meet across more rooms. Checking whether the people in a room are
"really there", keeping a list of rooms that went bad, or leaving and re-asking
are all answers to a platform defect that is fixed: ask once and play in what
comes back.

**A room has a maximum, not a starting line.** `seats` is the most people who
may sit down, and the room ticks from the first one: `step` is handed the seats
connected right now, so whether anything happens before the rest arrive is your
decision and not ours. Say it in two places -- `step` advances the state or
stands still, and `waiting` names the seats the match cannot go on without. A
page that cannot begin alone stands still and returns the empty seats from
`waiting`, which is how the person who is missing is told. A page people drop
into plays on and returns `[]`, because nobody is holding anything up.

## Seats

**Seats are numbered from 1.** `mine`, `turn`, `seated[].seat` and `next` all
count from 1. There is no seat 0, and a `next` that names one is refused.

**Seat 1 acts first**, from the moment the room opens.

```js
const piece = room.mine === 1 ? "X" : "O";   // never seat === 0
const myTurn = room.turn === room.mine;      // this, and nothing worked out from the board
```

`turn` is the one the server enforces. A page that derives whose move it is
from its own board has a second opinion that can disagree, and when it does the
page locks.

## The invitation

**The link is the invitation.** `state.link` is the room's link, ready to send:
whoever opens it joins that room, because a link joins by itself. Show it while
the room has an empty seat.

```js
mb.live.lobby((state) => {
  if (state.present && state.present.length < state.seats) showLink(state.link);
});
```

**Send `mb.shareUrl(...)` and never `location.href`.** Your page runs inside a
frame, and its own address carries a marker of ours. A link built from
`location.href` opens the page without the frame -- no panel, no sign-in, no
way into a seat. `shareUrl(extra)` gives the address the page is reachable at,
with our marker removed, your query kept, and what you pass set on top; `null`
for a key drops it.

**Put the room in the link and nothing else.** Every other value in a link is a
value the person you invited can edit before they open it.

A name you choose yourself is one room everybody on the page shares -- right
for a single open table, wrong for anything private.

**Or ask somebody by name, and we draw the card.**

```js
const asked = await mb.room.invite(room.name);
if (asked.sent) show("Invitation sent");        // asked.sent is a NUMBER
else show("Nobody was asked");                  // asked.closed, the card was dismissed
```

`mb.room.invite(name)` opens OUR sheet over your page: two lists the person
already knows -- who they sat down with, who they follow -- and a field that
takes a username. It resolves when the card closes.

**It takes no name and returns none.** You never send us an address, and the
answer is a count: `{ sent: 2 }`, or `{ closed: true }` when nothing went out.
Your page learns that a card was opened and how many invitations left it. There
is no list of people in this SDK and there will not be one.

**There is no accept step.** Whoever was asked takes a seat, and taking it is
the acceptance. Keep the link from `mb.shareUrl` as well: an invitation is one
way in and a link is the other.

## Accounts

**A guest can join an existing named room.** The default join gate permits
this. An invitation-only room refuses a guest. A guest cannot open a named
room or enter a resource room.

**A guest uses a pass, not a sign-in.** Their name is `guest_` and four
characters. The browser keeps the same guest for one day. `mb.viewer` still
reports that the person is not signed in. Their round result is recorded.

**A guest seat lasts while the guest is present.** After 60 seconds without
presence, another person can take it. A named account seat remains durable.
All public seats retain the presence rule above.

**You do not build a sign-in.** An ask to open a named room without an account
returns `refused.needsAccount`. The mindblown panel supplies the sign-in.
After sign-in, the person joins as their account. Your page draws the refusal
until that join succeeds.

**They may close the ask.** Then they are looking at your page with no seat --
a real state, and it has to work. Calling `mb.live.play` again brings the ask
back, so give them one control that means "play with somebody".

**Reading stays open.** `look` works signed out: who is here and what everybody
sees, with no seat and no hidden state.

## Testing it

**A page for two people cannot be tested by one person.** You take seat 1 and
wait, and nothing happens, because nothing can. So ask for a **test seat**: a
second person who exists for half an hour, in one room of one page.

**Do not say a page for two works until two people have met in it.** Running
`rules.js` on your own machine proves the rules and nothing else: not the
arrival from a link, not the join, not the start. Open two seat links, and the
page works when both of them see every seat connected.

Two doors, and the page must be the asker's own either way.

```
POST https://api.mindblown.ai/me/test-seats/<game_id>          you hold their session
Authorization: Bearer <the owner's access token>

POST https://api.mindblown.ai/internal/test-seats/<game_id>    you are their pod
Authorization: Bearer <the service token>
X-Mindblown-Subject: <the subject token naming the person>

{ "count": 1, "seats": 2 }      the pod's body also names "channel", "channel_id"
```

`channel` and `channel_id` must name an address that has written to the bot.
A lookup never creates a person.

The answer is one entry per test person:

```json
{
  "room": "quiet-lake-41",
  "ttl_seconds": 1800,
  "seats": [{
    "account_id": "...", "username": "test_9f2c1ab7", "name": "Tester 1",
    "seat": 2, "room": "quiet-lake-41", "pass": "...",
    "url": "https://mindblown.ai/...?mb_seat=<pass>&room=quiet-lake-41",
    "expires_at": "..."
  }]
}
```

**Open the `url` in a second window and that window is the second person.** It
joins, it is seen, it plays, it leaves. Your page needs no change and cannot
tell the difference: a test seat comes through the same door as anybody else.
Put the OWNER in the same `room` -- open your own page with `?room=<room>` --
and the two of them are at one table.

**What a test seat is.** A real account with a name and a seat, so everything
your page reads about a person is really there, `mb.viewer` included: it reads
as signed in. It holds a `pass`, not a session -- all that can do is take a
ticket for its own seat.

**What it is not.** It never appears in the people anybody played with, it is
never counted as somebody playing now, it has no inbox, and a match in a room
that held one is not written down. So a page is not made to look busy by being
tested, and a test does not end up in anybody's history.

**So a test seat cannot prove the RECORD** -- everything up to the end of a
match, but not what we wrote down. Check that with real accounts.

**Half an hour, then it is gone.** The account is deleted and its seat with it.
Ask again if you need longer; there is no way to extend one.

**Count what you need.** `count` is how many test people, `seats` is how big the
room is -- leave `seats` out and the room is built for your test people plus
you. Up to fifteen test seats, because a room holds sixteen.

**It is for testing and it is not a player.** Do not use test seats to make a
page look played, to fill a room a real person is waiting in, or to leave a
page running. Nothing stops you; the numbers simply will not move, because
none of them counts a test seat.

## `rules.js`

An ES module with five exports. Nothing about where it runs.

```js
export const config = { seats: 2, watch: true, hold: 60 };
export function init(seats, rng, context) { return state; }
export function step(state, inputs, dt, rng, seats) { return state; }
export function view(state, seat) { return whatThisSeatSees; }
export function waiting(state, seats) { return []; }   // seats the match cannot go on without
export function done(state) { return null; }   // or how it ended
```

| Export | Called | Arguments | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `config` | read by your page | -- | `{ seats, watch, hold }`. **Not yet enforced by the room**: the size is what `mb.room.join` opened the room with, and `watch` and `hold` are on the list below |
| `init` | before the first step without saved state | `seats`: connected seat numbers; `rng`; frozen `context` | the starting state |
| `step` | every tick | `state`; `inputs`: `{ [seat]: latestInput }` for seats that sent one this tick; `dt` in ms; `rng`; `seats` connected now | the next state, or nothing to mean "I changed it in place" |
| `view` | every tick, once per seat | `state`, `seat` | what that seat receives. JSON. |
| `waiting` | every tick, optional | `state`, `seats` connected | the seats the match cannot go on without. A turn-based file answers `[state.turn]`; a match that is simply on answers `[]`. It is how the platform knows to say "waiting for you" |
| `done` | every tick | `state` | falsy while the match is on; anything else is how it ended, sent to every seat and **written down**. See [What we keep](#what-we-keep) |

**Time and randomness come in as arguments.** `rng()` gives a number in
`[0, 1)` from a generator the room seeded; `dt` is ours. Use them. During a
tick the room also answers `Math.random()` from the same generator and
`Date.now()` with the tick's time, so a file that reads them can still be run
again from the room's log (see [What happened in a room](#what-happened-in-a-room)).

**`view` is where hidden information lives.** A hand, fog of war, a bluff:
return to seat 3 only what seat 3 may know. The room sends nothing a `view`
did not return. Everything in `state` that `view` returns to everybody is
public.

**Keep it small and keep it pure.** Under 512KB. No imports of anything but
your own code. A `step` that throws is reported to every seat on every tick
as `error`, in your own words, and the match stands still until it stops.

**`seats` is the list of seats connected right now**, in no particular
order. A seat whose socket dropped is absent from it and sends no input; a
seat that comes back is present again. `init` receives the seats present at
the first tick, which may be one -- a match that needs two waits in `step`
until `seats.length` says so.

**What `done` returns is recorded, and two shapes name a winner.** The room
reports the end once and the platform keeps it -- the seats, the accounts
behind them, how long it ran. Say `{ winner: 2 }` or `{ places: [2, 1, 3] }`
and the platform knows who finished where; add `{ scores: { "2": 40 } }` and it
knows what each seat scored. Anything else is kept whole and names nobody,
which is right for a match that has no winner. This is an offer and not a
requirement: the shape is yours, and these three are the parts we can read.

## `mb.live`

```js
mb.live.match((channel) => {                  // see The lobby and the match
  channel.send(input);                        // this seat's latest input
  const off = channel.on("tick", (tick) => draw(tick));
  channel.on("close", ({ code, reason }) => ...);
});
```

A `Channel`:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `seat` | your seat number, from 1 |
| `room` | the room: `name`, `seats`, `seated` with everybody named |
| `send(input)` | your input. Any JSON. Last write per tick wins, so one a tick is all a room can use -- see above |
| `on(event, fn)` | `"tick"` and `"close"`. Returns a function that unsubscribes |
| `close()` | closes the socket. The seat is still yours; `mb.live.leave()` gives it back |

**The page never holds the socket.** The mindblown panel on your page opens
it, with a ticket your page never sees, and relays what the room says. Your
page speaks to `channel` and nothing else.

### Immutable resources

Create a room from published documents when its rules need a fixed layout.
Each resource belongs to this page and remains unchanged during the attempt.

```js
const requestId = crypto.randomUUID();
const channel = await mb.live.create({
  seats: 2,
  resources: { vault: published.id },
  requestId,
});
channel.on("tick", (tick) => draw(tick));
```

Creation requires a real account and one through four published documents.
Their combined JSON must fit within 64 KiB.
The channel has the same methods as the one `match` hands you.
Keep `requestId` for an explicit retry after a lost response.
Retry the same request; different content produces `IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`.
An identical retry returns the original room without another seat replacement.
A superseded attempt can refuse its ticket with `NO_SEAT`.
The error preserves `requestId` and any room receipt already received.

The rules receive a frozen context before initialization:

```js
export function init(seats, rng, context) {
  const vault = context.resources.vault;
  return { cells: [...vault.value.cells], moves: 0 };
}
```

Each resource contains `id`, `kind`, `schemaVersion`, `hash`, and `value`.
Ordinary rooms receive `{resources:{}}`.
Saved state survives runtime recovery; recovery does not call `init` again.
The context stays inside the rules unless `view` returns part of it.

A resource room permits one completed attempt.
Its first `done` stops simulation and becomes the final result.
Reconnects receive the same final view and result.
Create another room for another attempt.
Owner removal lets an already-started attempt finish.
Platform removal can stop an attempt.
Temporary authorization failures pause simulation until access returns.

## The tick

Every seat receives, twenty times a second:

```js
{
  t: 1789371672003,   // the room's clock, ms
  tick: 4812,         // counts up from 1
  dt: 50,             // ms since the previous tick
  seats: [1, 2],      // who is connected right now
  waiting: [2],       // who the match cannot go on without, from waiting()
  view: { ... },      // what view(state, mySeat) returned
  done: null,         // or what done(state) returned
  error: "..."        // only when rules.js threw or could not be fetched
}
```

When `error` is present there is no `view`. Show the sentence; it is yours.

A late joiner's first tick is a whole view, so there is nothing to catch up
on. A room with sockets open and no input for three seconds stops ticking
until the next input; your page sees the gap as a pause, not as a fault.

**One socket per seat, and the newest window holds it.** A seat is a person and
joining twice is the same seat, so a second tab, a reload that raced its own
close and a reconnect after a drop all ask for a seat that already has a socket.
The room hands it to the newest and tells the old one `{ closed: "elsewhere" }`
before closing it. Two consequences worth designing for: `seats` never carries
the same number twice, so `seats.length` is a count of PEOPLE; and one person
cannot fill two seats by opening two windows -- to test a match with two
players you need two accounts.

**The view is the budget, and it is the only one you are likely to reach.** The
room sends one to every seat twenty times a second, so a view is paid for
sixteen hundred times a minute at eight seats. Two measurements, both from real
pages: a page that returns the whole board with the parts a seat cannot see set
to `null` sent 5.9KB per seat per tick -- about 1MB a second at eight seats --
and a page that culled by line of sight inside `view` sent 333 bytes, which is
52KB a second. The difference is twenty-fold.

**So cull in `view`, not in the page.** It already exists to decide what one
seat may see, which makes it the only place that can leave something out
honestly -- a page that filters what it draws still downloaded the rest, and a
page that could read it could cheat with it. If a visibility test is expensive,
work it out once per tick rather than once per pair. One page's went from 56
traces to 28, and the cost of a whole tick's views fell from 0.615ms to
0.015ms.

**What the room itself can carry is not the constraint you will meet first.**
Measured against the live room, with a page that culls inside `view`:

| seats | inputs each | ticks a second | gap, typical | gap, worst |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 15 | 19.8 | 49ms | 68ms |
| 8 | 15 | 20.1 | 50ms | 81ms |
| 8 | 30 | 20.0 | 49ms | 81ms |
| 16 | 30 | 20.0 | 50ms | 102ms |
| 16 | 60 | 20.0 | 50ms | 83ms |

Every message on the wire in those runs was around 464 bytes, envelope and all,
and it did not grow when the input rate doubled. The last row is twice the rate
any page should send, at the seat cap, and it is 960 messages a second into one
room -- the ceiling the platform gives us -- with the clock still at 50ms. Rerun
it yourself with `mindblown-live/probe.mjs`; a number in a document nobody can
reproduce goes stale without anybody noticing.

## Turns on live

A turn-based match is a rules file whose `step` listens to one seat. There is
no other machinery: `state.turn` is a number your `step` moves along, hidden
hands are what `view` keeps back, and `waiting` names the seat whose move it
is so the platform can say so. The room enforces all of it -- nobody moves out
of turn, nobody moves twice, nobody sees a hand that is not theirs -- because
the room is the only thing running the file.

Noughts and crosses, whole:

```js
export const config = { seats: 2, watch: true, hold: 60 };
export function init(seats, rng) { return { cells: Array(9).fill(0), turn: 1, moves: 0 }; }
const LINES = [[0,1,2],[3,4,5],[6,7,8],[0,3,6],[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[0,4,8],[2,4,6]];
const winner = (c) => LINES.map(([a, b, d]) => c[a] && c[a] === c[b] && c[a] === c[d] ? c[a] : 0).find(Boolean) || 0;
export function step(state, inputs, dt, rng, seats) {
  if (winner(state.cells) || state.moves === 9) return state;
  const input = inputs[state.turn];                       // one seat is heard
  if (!input || !Number.isInteger(input.cell) || input.cell < 0 || input.cell > 8) return state;
  if (state.cells[input.cell]) return state;
  state.cells[input.cell] = state.turn;
  state.moves++;
  state.turn = state.turn === 1 ? 2 : 1;
  return state;
}
export function view(state, seat) { return { me: seat, cells: state.cells, turn: state.turn }; }
export function waiting(state) { return winner(state.cells) || state.moves === 9 ? [] : [state.turn]; }
export function done(state) {
  const w = winner(state.cells);
  return w ? { winner: w } : state.moves === 9 ? { draw: true } : null;
}
```

A card table is the same shape with a `deck` array in `state`, shuffled with
`rng` in `init`, dealt by `step`, and hidden by `view` -- return to seat 3 only
`state.hands[3]`. A trade is `step` moving items between two hands when the
seat holding the turn asks. A showdown is `view` no longer hiding. A deadline
is a number in `state` compared with the tick's clock.

The page for a turn-based match sends its move once, on the tap, and draws on the
tick. It does not need thirty inputs a second.

**The old turn-based wire** -- `mb.room.look` and `mb.room.act` with `next`,
`hold`, `deck`, `deal`, `give`, `take`, `show` -- is deprecated as of
2026-09-15. It keeps answering for the pages already on it until 31 December
2026 and is written down at the end of this file. New pages write the file
above.

## Drawing between ticks

Twenty ticks a second is not sixty frames. Draw at your frame rate. A page
that draws only on ticks looks like twenty frames a second, because it is.
How to draw between ticks depends on who moves the thing.

**What the room moves, interpolate.** A board, a score, anything `step`
moves: keep the previous view and its `t`, and draw a point `dt`-proportional
between the last two. It is drawn about one tick late, and that is right,
because the room is the authority on it.

**What another seat moves, draw where it is NOW, not where it was.** When each
seat sends its own position -- a vehicle, a body, a pointer -- the newest
sample you hold for another seat is already old when it arrives. Every frame,
carry it forward: its position plus its velocity times the sample's age, with
its turn rate if you send one. When the next sample arrives, blend toward it
over about 100ms rather than jumping. Stop carrying it forward after about
250ms without a sample, and hold it where it is, so a dropped seat does not
drive off on its own. Send each sample with its time on the room's clock (the
last tick's `t` plus the time since that tick), so the other page knows how
old it is.

**Do not hold samples back to smooth them.** A buffer that draws other seats
some milliseconds in the past adds all of those milliseconds to what a person
sees, however fast the delivery under it is.

**Prediction is optional and it is the same file.** A page may `import`
`/rules.js` itself and run `step` locally with its own input to draw ahead
of the next tick, then snap to the view when it arrives. Start without it.

## What we decide

Ours, and no page can change it:

- **who you are** -- the seat comes from a ticket the API signed, never from
  a message,
- **what you can see** -- `view` is applied by the room, never by a page,
- **the clock** -- `dt` is ours; nobody runs their own faster,
- **the dice** -- `rng` is ours and seeded,
- **which rules** -- the file at your host when the room opened. A republish
  never changes a match in progress; the next room gets the new file.

Yours: whether `step` is right. We do not know your rules. What we know is
that every seat is running the same ones.

## What we keep

These rematch rules apply to ordinary rooms. Resource rooms permit one completed attempt.

**`done` is how a round is written down, and a room that never ends keeps
nothing.** When `done` returns something, the room reports it and we record the
match: who held each seat, how long it ran, and the result whole. When `done`
goes falsy again the room has started another one, it gets the next sequence,
and that one is recorded too. **So a page with rounds should end each round
through `done` and let the next begin — not return `null` for ever.**

```js
export function done(state) {
  // the ROUND ended, and the room plays on
  if (state.round.over) return { places: state.round.order };
  return null;
}
```

A file that answers `null` for ever is a file we hold no history for. Measured
2026-09-18: a page that had been played for hours in dozens of rounds had
**zero** records, because its `done` said `return null; // the room never ends`.

**Return `places`, not only `scores`.** `places` is the finishing order —
`[3, 1, 2]` means seat 3 came first — and it is the one thing that means the
same in every page. A score is yours: two hundred is a triumph in one page and
a rout in another, so nothing can compare it with anything. Both are kept, and
`winner` is accepted as shorthand for a single first place:

| in the result | what we do with it |
| --- | --- |
| `places: [3, 1, 2]` | seat 3 first, seat 1 second, seat 2 third |
| `winner: 2` | seat 2 first, everybody else unplaced |
| `scores: { "1": 240, "2": 90 }` | kept per seat, compared with nothing |

Anything else stays in the raw result and names no winner.
Read your account's recorded outcomes with `mb.matches.list({limit:20})`.
The reply contains `{items,nextCursor}`.
Each item includes your outcomes, match times, room, sequence, and available resource provenance.
Pass `nextCursor` to read the next page.
Only exact account bindings appear. Test rooms and inferred participation remain excluded.
Other accounts' outcomes and raw result JSON remain private.

## What happened in a room

**A room writes down every tick as your rules saw it**: the tick's number, its
time, `dt`, the seats in order, every seat's input, and a digest of every view.
With the room's seed and the state where the log starts, that is enough to run
the room again, tick for tick. A room keeps the last hour.


Only the page's owner reads a room's log (`GET /me/rooms/{page_id}/{room}/log`).
It holds nothing your rules file was not already given.

## Who is watching

Each seat carries `online` and `seen` -- seconds since that person's page last
asked about the room. Presence is the heartbeat of `look`; nothing to send.

**Presence is not membership.** Somebody offline still holds their seat. Show
it; do not free a seat because a tab closed.

```js
room.seated.forEach((s) =>
  mark(s.seat, s.username, s.online ? "here" : `away ${Math.round(s.seen / 60)}m`));
```

## Names on screen

A few views of a page are recorded, so its maker can watch how it is used.
People's names and what they send each other never reach a recording: we black
them out wherever we can see them drawn -- HTML text, and `fillText` on a
canvas in the page.

Text you draw in 3D -- a name over a car, a chat line on a texture, a font
atlas -- we cannot see. A room page with a 3D canvas is then not recorded at
all, unless you say where the names are:

```js
mb.recording.mask((canvas) => {
  // CSS pixels of this canvas; [] when no name is on screen.
  return labels.filter((l) => l.visible).map((l) => ({ x: l.x - 4, y: l.y - 4, width: l.w + 8, height: l.h + 8 }));
});
```

Return every rectangle a name or a message covers this frame. Return `null`
to leave a frame out. Calling it costs nothing when the view is not recorded.

## Refusals

A refusal reaches the lobby as `state.refused.reason`:

| `reason` | what happened | what to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NO_SEAT` | the seat was lost before the socket opened | call `mb.live.play` again |
| `OPENED_ELSEWHERE` | the same person opened this room in another window | say so; that window has the seat |
| `ROOM_UNREACHABLE` | the room closed five times before the match began | offer `mb.live.play` again |
| `ROOM_CLOSED` | the room has ended | show the result |
| `BAD_ASK` | the room name or page id was malformed | a bug in the page |
| `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` | live rooms are off on this deployment | say so; the turn-based room still works |

An `error` on a tick is not a refusal: the socket is open and the room is
telling you your file is broken.

And `ROOM_FULL` (every seat taken), `ROOM_SIZE` (a room seats 2 to 16, and a
new one has to say) and `NOT_INVITED` (a private room its opener keeps to the
people they invite).

## Not yet built, said plainly

- `config.watch` and `config.hold` are read by nobody yet. Spectators cannot
  connect; a dropped seat is simply absent from `seats` until it returns.
- `waiting` reaches every seat on the tick, and the room now tells the platform
  which seats a match has waited on for a minute. The inbox that shows it to
  somebody who is away is being built.
- A key can be rotated; it has not been.

## A whole page

mindblown adds `window.mindblown` to every page when it publishes it, so the
page loads nothing for it.

```html
<canvas id="c" width="400" height="300"></canvas>
<div id="lobby"></div>
<button id="play">Play with somebody</button>
<script>
const mb = window.mindblown;
let last = null;

mb.live.lobby((state) => {
  const box = document.getElementById("lobby");
  if (state.refused) { box.textContent = state.refused.needsAccount ? "Sign in to play" : state.refused.reason; return; }
  const here = state.present.map((p) => p.username || "seat " + p.seat).join(", ");
  box.textContent = here + " -- waiting for " + (state.seats - state.present.length) + ". " + state.link;
});

mb.live.match((channel) => {
  document.getElementById("lobby").textContent = "";
  channel.on("tick", (tick) => { last = tick; });
  let dy = 0;
  addEventListener("keydown", (e) => { dy = e.key === "ArrowUp" ? -1 : e.key === "ArrowDown" ? 1 : dy; });
  addEventListener("keyup", () => { dy = 0; });
  setInterval(() => channel.send({ dy }), 1000 / 20);
  requestAnimationFrame(function frame() { draw(last); requestAnimationFrame(frame); });
});

document.getElementById("play").onclick = () => mb.live.play({ public: true, seats: 2 });
</script>
```

A person who opens the link lands in the room with no click. A person who
presses the button is put with somebody. Both see the same lobby, and the match
starts for both when the second one connects.

## The old wire, until 31 December 2026

`mb.room.look` and `mb.room.act`, and the server operations under them, were
how a turn-based match was played before the rules ran on the server. They are
deprecated as of 2026-09-15: every answer carries a `Deprecation` header, and
they keep answering for the pages already written on them. **Do not write a new
page against anything in this section** -- the file under "Turns on live" does
all of it, and the room enforces it.

### A turn

```js
await mb.room.act(room.name, {
  move:  { played: "ace" },   // yours. We never read it
  state: { pile: 3 },         // patches what everybody sees
  mine:  { note: "hello" },   // patches what only you see
  next:  2,                   // hand the turn to a seat
  hold:  30,                  // seconds before anybody may take it back
  close: true,                // end the room
});
```

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `move` | recorded in the log as sent. Never read by us |
| `state`, `mine` | **patches**: a key you send replaces that key, a key you leave out is untouched |
| `next` | where the turn goes. Leave it out and it goes to the next seat. Only the seat holding the turn may direct it |
| `hold` | seconds the next seat has before anybody seated may act. Reported back as `turn_until`. Leave it out and the turn waits as long as it needs |
| `close` | ends the room. No further turns |

**Send `hold` whenever you hand the turn to somebody who might not answer.** A
seat holding the turn is holding the room; if they close the tab, it stops for
everybody. Past `hold`, taking the turn is the same call as using it, and the
log shows who took it.

**`next` is every order but plain rotation** -- a skip, a reversal, a second
turn, or handing the turn to the person you are trading with so they can
answer.

### What we decide

Things a page must not decide for itself, because the other seats could not
check it:

```js
await mb.room.act(room.name, {
  roll: { dice: 2, sides: 6, as: "throw" },            // we throw them
  deck: { key: "bank", items: [...], shuffle: true },  // a supply nobody reads
  deal: { from: "bank", to: 3, key: "hand", count: 2 },
  give: { to: 1, key: "hand", items: ["ore"] },        // out of YOUR hand
  take: { from: 2, to: 1, key: "hand", count: 1 },     // nobody chooses which
  show: { key: "hand", as: "hand2" },                  // turn YOUR hand face up
});
```

| Field | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `roll` | dice. The result lands in `state[as]` as `{ dice, total }`, public |
| `deck` | loads a supply into the room. It is in no answer to anybody |
| `deal` | moves the top `count` of a supply into a seat's hidden state |
| `give` | moves named items out of **your own** hidden state to another seat |
| `take` | moves `count` items nobody chooses from one seat to another |
| `show` | copies **your own** hidden key into the public state |

**A key we have written is a key you may not write.** Once `deal`, `give` or
`take` has touched `hand`, a `mine` patch to `hand` is refused. Keys we never
touched stay yours.

**A trade is two gives and a handover.** Give what you offer, `next` to the
other person, they give back and hand the turn on.

**Hidden dice are a deck, not a roll.** `roll` is public by design. For dice
only one seat may see, load a deck of faces and `deal` from it.

#### The showdown

**A reveal is ours or it settles nothing.** A page can print anything; `show`
is the server publishing the hand it dealt, and the log says so.

```js
await mb.room.act(room.name, { show: { key: "dice", as: "dice" + room.mine } });
```

- `as` gives every seat its own public key. Without it the hand lands under its
  own name and four seats showing at once overwrite each other.
- **A bare `show` does not wait for your turn.** It moves nothing, patches
  nothing, and leaves the turn and its deadline where they are. A `show` with
  anything else beside it is an ordinary turn, refused with `NOT_YOUR_TURN`
  when it is not yours.
- Showing a key you were never dealt is `NOT_HELD`.
- A show is a copy; the hand stays in `private`.

#### What is guaranteed

Ours, and no page can talk us out of it: who you are (the seat comes from the
session), when you may act, what you can see, what a die landed on and how a
deck was shuffled, and the order of the log.

Yours: whether a legal-looking move is a right move. `state` is public and the
log is shared, so every copy of your page can check the table against it.

### Staying up to date

```js
let seq = room.seq;
for (;;) {
  const now = await mb.room.look(room.name, { since: seq, wait: 25 });
  seq = now.seq;
  now.moves.forEach(apply);
}
```

`wait` holds the answer until the room moves -- somebody acts, somebody takes
a seat, the turn changes hands -- or the seconds run out; a quiet room answers
on the deadline with what it has. Thirty is the most we hold. Without `wait`,
poll every second or two.

This was the old wire's poll. A match runs on the tick now; see
[The tick](#the-tick).
